title: Skunk Ape Research Headquarters
summary: The roadside attraction in the Florida Everglades dedicated to hunting the Skunk Ape - Florida's version of Bigfoot, supposedly seven feet tall, covered in hair, and smelling like a mixture of garbage, skunk, and swamp.

content.intro: On the Tamiami Trail through the Everglades, between Miami and Naples, a hand-painted sign advertises the Skunk Ape Research Headquarters. Inside, amid taxidermied alligators and live reptiles, Dave Shealy has spent decades searching for the Skunk Ape - Florida's stinky cousin of Bigfoot. The Skunk Ape is supposedly seven feet tall, covered in reddish-brown hair, and distinguished by an overwhelming odor: part skunk, part garbage, part swamp. Sightings date back to the 1960s. Shealy claims to have seen the creature twice and has captured it on video (blurry, obviously). His research headquarters is equal parts cryptid museum, reptile zoo, and roadside attraction. Whether you believe in the Skunk Ape or not, Shealy's dedication is genuine. He's spent 40 years in the swamp looking for something most scientists say doesn't exist. The Everglades are vast and wild enough that believers can always say: 'But what if...?'

sections.title: The Creature
sections.body: The Skunk Ape reportedly stands six to seven feet tall, walks upright, and is covered in dark reddish-brown hair. Its most distinctive feature is its smell - an overwhelming stench that witnesses compare to rotting garbage, sulfur, and skunk. Sightings cluster in the Big Cypress Swamp and Everglades, areas of dense subtropical wilderness that remain largely unexplored. Some witnesses report the creature living in alligator dens; others claim it feeds on deer and wild hogs. Unlike Bigfoot sightings in the Pacific Northwest, Skunk Ape encounters often emphasize the smell first - witnesses describe being overwhelmed by the odor before seeing anything.

sections.title: The Researcher
sections.body: Dave Shealy grew up in the Everglades - his family ran a campground on the Tamiami Trail. He saw his first Skunk Ape at age 10, he claims, and has been searching ever since. In 1998, he opened the Skunk Ape Research Headquarters as both a base of operations and a tourist attraction. Shealy has collected hundreds of eyewitness accounts, installed trail cameras throughout the swamp, and produced videos he claims show the creature (skeptics see a person in a suit). He's appeared on numerous television shows about cryptids. Whether he's a true believer or a savvy businessman depends on your perspective. Probably he's both.

sections.title: The Headquarters
sections.body: The Skunk Ape Research Headquarters is a classic Florida roadside attraction. The building is festooned with hand-painted signs and Skunk Ape imagery. Inside, displays explain the creature's history, present eyewitness evidence, and sell merchandise. A small zoo houses alligators, snakes, and other Everglades wildlife. Shealy offers swamp buggy tours into the surrounding wilderness, where visitors can search for evidence themselves. The gift shop sells Skunk Ape t-shirts, coffee mugs, and plaster footprint casts. Admission is cheap; the experience is genuine Old Florida kitsch, the kind that's increasingly rare as chains replace independent attractions.

sections.title: The Science
sections.body: Scientists are skeptical of the Skunk Ape for the same reasons they're skeptical of Bigfoot: no body has ever been found, no clear photographs exist, and the reported creature would require a breeding population to survive - meaning hundreds or thousands of individuals somehow avoiding documentation in one of America's most studied ecosystems. Skeptics note that Florida has black bears, which can stand upright and might be misidentified. The smell could be decomposing vegetation, natural gas seeps, or the witness's own imagination. But the Everglades are vast - 1.5 million acres of swamp, cypress stands, and sawgrass that humans rarely penetrate. Believers argue that something could hide there.

sections.title: Visiting Skunk Ape Research Headquarters
sections.body: The Skunk Ape Research Headquarters is located at 40904 Tamiami Trail East (US-41) in Ochopee, Florida, about 35 miles west of Miami and 35 miles east of Naples. The facility is open daily; admission is charged. Swamp buggy tours are available. The adjacent area includes Big Cypress National Preserve and Everglades National Park - both worth exploring. The Ochopee Post Office, the smallest in America, is nearby. The Tamiami Trail drive is scenic, cutting through wetlands and offering wildlife viewing. Miami International Airport and Southwest Florida International Airport (Fort Myers) are equidistant. Bug spray is essential. The Skunk Ape has never been photographed clearly; the alligators definitely exist.

content.flightContext: Located at 25.86°N, 81.30°W on the Tamiami Trail in the western Everglades, Florida. From altitude, the area is vast wetland - sawgrass marsh, cypress domes, and open water stretching to every horizon. The Tamiami Trail (US-41) cuts a straight line through the wilderness. The Research Headquarters is a small roadside facility, barely visible amid the swamp. Big Cypress National Preserve surrounds the area. Miami is 35 miles east; Naples is 35 miles west. The isolation is genuine - this is one of the last great wildernesses in the eastern United States. Miami International Airport is the nearest major commercial service.
